sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 15
title: Calculating Velocity of a Falling Object: A Rock Thrown Down
statement: What happens if the person on the cliff throws the rock straight down, instead of straight up? To explore this question, calculate the velocity of the rock when it is 5.10 m below the starting point, and has been thrown downward with an initial speed of 13.0 m/s.

givenValues.description: final position (negative because below starting point)

solution.approach: Use the kinematic equation that relates velocity, position, and acceleration without time: v² = v₀² + 2a(y - y₀)
steps: Set up the kinematic equation: v² = v₀² + 2a(y - y₀)
Substitute known values: v² = (-13.0)² + 2(-9.80)(-5.10 - 0)
Simplify: v² = 169 + 99.96
Continue: v² = 268.96
Take square root: v = ±\sqrt{268.96} = ±16.4 m/s
Since the rock is moving downward, choose the negative value: v = -16.4 m/s

hints.hint: Remember that up is positive, so downward motion and positions below the starting point are negative.
Use the kinematic equation v² = v₀² + 2a(y - y₀) since it doesn't involve time.
When taking the square root, choose the negative value since the rock continues moving downward.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 1 (Reaction Time Experiment)
title: Reaction Time and Stopping Distance
statement: A simple experiment can be done to determine your reaction time. Have a friend hold a ruler between your thumb and index finger, separated by about 1 cm. Note the mark on the ruler that is right between your fingers. Have your friend drop the ruler unexpectedly, and try to catch it between your two fingers. Note the new reading on the ruler. Assuming acceleration is that due to gravity, calculate your reaction time. How far would you travel in a car (moving at 30 m/s) if the time it took your foot to go from the gas pedal to the brake was twice this reaction time?

solution.approach: Use kinematic equation for free fall to find reaction time, then calculate stopping distance
steps: Let Δy be the distance the ruler falls during reaction time
Using kinematic equation: Δy = v₀t + \frac{1}{2}gt²
Since v₀ = 0: Δy = \frac{1}{2}gt²
Solving for t: t = \sqrt{\frac{2Δy}{g}}
For typical ruler drop of ~20 cm: t = \sqrt{\frac{2(0.20)}{9.80}} = \sqrt{0.0408} = 0.20 s
Brake reaction time = 2 × 0.20 s = 0.40 s
Distance = v × t = 30 m/s × 0.40 s = 12 m
solution.finalAnswer: Reaction time ≈ 0.20 s, stopping distance = 12 m

hints.hint: The ruler undergoes free fall motion with initial velocity zero
Use the kinematic equation relating distance, time, and acceleration
The brake reaction time is twice the measured reaction time

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 2 (Finding g from Falling Object)
title: Determining g from Experimental Data
statement: An object, usually a metal ball for which air resistance is negligible, is dropped and the time it takes to fall a known distance is measured. Suppose the ball falls 1.0000 m in 0.45173 s. Assuming the ball is not affected by air resistance, what is the precise acceleration due to gravity at this location?

solution.approach: Use kinematic equation to solve for acceleration
steps: Choose kinematic equation: Δy = v₀t + \frac{1}{2}at²
Since v₀ = 0: Δy = \frac{1}{2}at²
Solve for a: a = \frac{2Δy}{t²}
Substitute known values: a = \frac{2(-1.0000)}{(0.45173)²}
Therefore: g = 9.8058 m/s²
solution.finalAnswer: g = 9.81 m/s² (considering significant figures)

hints.hint: The object starts from rest, so initial velocity is zero
Use the kinematic equation that relates displacement, time, and acceleration
The negative sign indicates downward direction; g is the magnitude

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 3 (Ice Chunk Free Fall)
title: Ice Chunk Falling from Glacier
statement: A chunk of ice breaks off a glacier and falls 30.0 meters before it hits the water. Assuming it falls freely (there is no air resistance), how long does it take to hit the water?

solution.approach: Use kinematic equation to find time of fall
steps: Use kinematic equation: y = y₀ + v₀t + \frac{1}{2}at²
With downward as negative: y = 0 + 0 + \frac{1}{2}(-g)t²
Simplify: y = -\frac{1}{2}gt²
Substitute values: -30.0 = -\frac{1}{2}(9.80)t²
Take positive square root: t = \sqrt{6.122} = 2.47 s

hints.hint: The ice starts from rest and falls under gravity alone
Use the kinematic equation that doesn't involve final velocity
Take the positive square root since time cannot be negative

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 4 (Average Velocity from Graph)
title: Average Velocity from Position-Time Graph
statement: Find the average velocity of a jet-powered car whose position is given by the following data points from a position versus time graph: at t = 0.50 s, x = 525 m; at t = 6.40 s, x = 2000 m.

solution.approach: Calculate slope of position vs time graph
steps: Average velocity equals slope of position vs time graph
v_avg = \frac{Δx}{Δt} = \frac{x₂ - x₁}{t₂ - t₁}
Calculate displacement: Δx = 2000 m - 525 m = 1475 m
Calculate time interval: Δt = 6.40 s - 0.50 s = 5.90 s
Calculate average velocity: v_avg = \frac{1475 m}{5.90 s} = 250 m/s
solution.finalAnswer: v_avg = 250 m/s

hints.hint: Average velocity is the slope of the position versus time graph
Use the formula: average velocity = change in position / change in time
Make sure to use final values minus initial values for the changes

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 1
title: Finding Acceleration from Velocity-Time Graph Using Tangent Line
statement: Find the tangent line to the curve at t = 25 s. Determine the endpoints of the tangent. These correspond to a position of 1300 m at time 19 s and a position of 3120 m at time 32 s. Plug these endpoints into the equation to solve for the slope.

solution.approach: Find the slope of the tangent line to the velocity-time curve, which represents acceleration.
steps: The slope of a velocity vs. time graph represents acceleration: a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}
From the given endpoints, calculate the change in velocity: \Delta v = v_2 - v_1
Since we have positions, we need to interpret these as velocities at the tangent points
Calculate the time interval: \Delta t = t_2 - t_1 = 32 - 19 = 13 \text{ s}
If interpreting the values as velocities: \Delta v = 3120 - 1300 = 1820 \text{ m/s}
Calculate acceleration: a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{1820}{13} = 140 \text{ m/s}^2
solution.finalAnswer: a = 140 m/s²

hints.hint: The slope of a velocity vs. time graph gives acceleration.
Use the slope formula: slope = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}
The tangent line represents the instantaneous rate of change at that point.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 2
title: Calculating Acceleration from Velocity-Time Graph at t = 25s
statement: Calculate the acceleration of the jet car at a time of 25 s by finding the slope of the v vs. t graph. The slope of the curve at t = 25s is equal to the slope of the line tangent at that point. Determine endpoints of the tangent line from the figure, and then plug them into the equation to solve for slope.

givenValues.description: time at which to find acceleration

solution.approach: Find the slope of the tangent line to the velocity-time curve at t = 25s to determine instantaneous acceleration.
steps: Identify that acceleration is the slope of a velocity vs. time graph: a = \frac{dv}{dt}
At a specific point, this becomes the slope of the tangent line at that point
From the graph, determine two points on the tangent line at t = 25s
Apply the slope formula: a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{t_2 - t_1}
Substitute the values from the tangent line endpoints
Calculate the final acceleration value
solution.finalAnswer: The acceleration depends on the specific tangent line endpoints read from the graph.

hints.hint: The instantaneous acceleration equals the slope of the tangent line to the v-t curve.
Read coordinates of two points on the tangent line from the graph.
Use slope = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} where rise is change in velocity and run is change in time.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Conceptual Question 1
title: Distinguishing Distance, Displacement, and Magnitude of Displacement
statement: Give an example in which there are clear distinctions among distance traveled, displacement, and magnitude of displacement. Specifically identify each quantity in your example.

solution.approach: Provide a concrete example that illustrates the differences between these three related but distinct quantities.
steps: Consider a person walking from home to school (2 km east), then to a friend's house (1 km west of school), then back home
Distance traveled = total path length = 2 km + 1 km + 1 km = 4 km
Displacement = final position - initial position = 0 km (returned to starting point)
Magnitude of displacement = |displacement| = |0| = 0 km
This example shows: distance traveled (4 km) ≠ magnitude of displacement (0 km) ≠ displacement (0 km with no direction needed since magnitude is zero)
solution.finalAnswer: Example: Walking from home → school (2 km east) → friend's house (1 km west of school) → home. Distance traveled = 4 km, Displacement = 0 km, Magnitude of displacement = 0 km.

hints.hint: Think of a path that involves changing direction or returning to the starting point.
Distance is the total path length, displacement is the straight-line change in position.
Magnitude of displacement is always positive and equals the absolute value of displacement.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Conceptual Question 2
title: When Distance Traveled Equals Magnitude of Displacement
statement: Under what circumstances does distance traveled equal magnitude of displacement? What is the only case in which magnitude of displacement and displacement are exactly the same?

solution.approach: Analyze the geometric and directional conditions required for these equalities.
steps: Distance traveled equals magnitude of displacement when the object moves in a straight line in one direction only
This occurs when there is no change in direction and no backtracking
Magnitude of displacement equals displacement only when displacement is positive (or zero)
Since magnitude is always non-negative, displacement must be non-negative
This happens when the final position is in the positive direction from the initial position (using the chosen coordinate system)
solution.finalAnswer: Distance traveled = magnitude of displacement when motion is in a straight line in one direction. Magnitude of displacement = displacement only when displacement is positive (object moves in positive direction).

hints.hint: Consider what happens when you move in a straight line without changing direction.
Remember that magnitude is always positive or zero.
Think about coordinate systems and positive/negative directions.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Conceptual Question 4
title: Speed vs Velocity - Bird Diving Example
statement: A student writes, 'A bird that is diving for prey has a speed of 10 m/s downward.' What is wrong with the student's statement? What has the student actually described? Explain.

solution.approach: Identify the conceptual error in confusing speed with velocity.
steps: Speed is a scalar quantity - it has magnitude only, no direction
The student included a direction ('downward') with speed, which is incorrect
When a direction is specified with a magnitude, this describes velocity, not speed
The student has actually described the bird's velocity: 10 m/s downward
The correct speed would be simply: 10 m/s (no direction)
solution.finalAnswer: The student incorrectly gave a direction with speed. Speed is scalar (magnitude only). The student actually described velocity (10 m/s downward). The speed should be stated as simply 10 m/s.

hints.hint: Remember the difference between scalar and vector quantities.
Speed has no direction; velocity has both magnitude and direction.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 6
title: Vector Nature of Acceleration
statement: Acceleration is the change in velocity over time. Given this information, is acceleration a vector or a scalar quantity? Explain.

solution.approach: Analyze the definition of acceleration and the vector nature of velocity to determine if acceleration is a vector or scalar quantity.
steps: Recall that acceleration is defined as the change in velocity over time: $\vec{a} = \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}$
Note that velocity is a vector quantity (has both magnitude and direction)
When we calculate the change in velocity ($\Delta \vec{v}$), we are finding the vector difference between two velocity vectors
Dividing a vector by a scalar (time) results in a vector quantity
Therefore, acceleration must be a vector quantity
solution.finalAnswer: Acceleration is a vector quantity because it is defined as the change in velocity (which is a vector) divided by time (a scalar). Since the change in velocity is a vector operation and dividing by a scalar preserves the vector nature, acceleration has both magnitude and direction.

hints.hint: Think about whether velocity is a vector or scalar quantity.
Consider what happens when you divide a vector by a scalar.
Remember that acceleration can change the direction of motion, not just the speed.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 7
title: Temperature as Scalar or Vector
statement: A weather forecast states that the temperature is predicted to be 25°C the following day. Is this temperature a vector or a scalar quantity? Explain.

solution.approach: Determine whether temperature requires direction information or only magnitude to be completely specified.
steps: Consider what information is needed to completely specify temperature
Temperature only requires a magnitude (numerical value with units) to be completely described
Temperature does not have an associated direction in space
Compare with vector quantities like velocity or force that require both magnitude and direction
solution.finalAnswer: Temperature is a scalar quantity because it only has magnitude (25°C) and no directional component. It is completely specified by a single numerical value with appropriate units.

hints.hint: Does temperature have a direction associated with it?
Think about what information you need to completely describe temperature.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 8
title: Time Measurement Devices
statement: Give an example (but not one from the text) of a device used to measure time and identify what change in that device indicates a change in time.

solution.approach: Identify a common time-measuring device and explain how its physical change corresponds to time passage.
steps: Consider common time-measuring devices: digital clock, analog clock, stopwatch, hourglass, pendulum clock, etc.
Choose a specific example and identify the physical change that occurs
Example: Digital wristwatch - the change is the advancement of numbers on the display
Alternative example: Pendulum clock - the change is the oscillation of the pendulum and movement of clock hands
Explain how this change is calibrated to standard time units

Consider what physically changes in the device as time passes.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 9
title: Average Speed vs. Magnitude of Average Velocity
statement: There is a distinction between average speed and the magnitude of average velocity. Give an example that illustrates the difference between these two quantities.

solution.approach: Create a scenario where the path taken affects the total distance but not the displacement, showing how average speed and magnitude of average velocity differ.
steps: Define average speed = total distance traveled / total time
Define magnitude of average velocity = |displacement| / total time
Create example: A person walks from home to school (1 km north) in 10 minutes, then returns home (1 km south) in 10 minutes
Calculate total distance = 1 km + 1 km = 2 km
Calculate displacement = 0 km (ended at starting point)
Average speed = 2 km / 20 min = 0.1 km/min
Magnitude of average velocity = 0 km / 20 min = 0 km/min
solution.finalAnswer: Example: A student walks 1 km north from home to school in 10 minutes, then walks 1 km south back home in 10 minutes. Average speed = (total distance)/(total time) = 2 km/20 min = 0.1 km/min. Magnitude of average velocity = |displacement|/total time = 0 km/20 min = 0 km/min. The difference occurs because average speed uses total distance traveled while average velocity uses net displacement.

hints.hint: Think about a round trip where you end up where you started.
Consider how total distance differs from displacement.
Remember that displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 10
title: Odometer vs. Speedometer Measurements
statement: Does a car's odometer measure distance traveled or displacement? Does its speedometer measure speed or velocity?

solution.approach: Analyze what each instrument actually measures based on their design and function.
steps: Consider what an odometer measures: it tracks the total path length traveled by the wheels
An odometer accumulates distance regardless of direction changes or turns
Displacement would require knowing the straight-line distance from start to finish
Consider what a speedometer measures: it shows the magnitude of instantaneous velocity
A speedometer shows how fast you're going but not the direction of motion
Velocity requires both magnitude and direction information
solution.finalAnswer: A car's odometer measures distance traveled (the total path length), not displacement (straight-line distance from start to finish). A car's speedometer measures speed (magnitude of velocity), not velocity itself, because it doesn't indicate the direction of motion.

hints.hint: Think about whether these instruments provide directional information.
Consider what happens to the odometer reading when you drive in circles.
Remember that velocity is a vector quantity requiring both magnitude and direction.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 11
title: Calculating Average Speed vs. Average Velocity Magnitude
statement: If you divide the total distance traveled on a car trip (as determined by the odometer) by the time for the trip, are you calculating the average speed or the magnitude of the average velocity? Under what circumstances are these two quantities the same?

solution.approach: Analyze the calculation method and determine when average speed equals the magnitude of average velocity.
steps: Identify what is being calculated: total distance / total time = average speed
Compare with magnitude of average velocity = |displacement| / total time
For these to be equal: total distance must equal magnitude of displacement
This occurs when the path taken is a straight line from start to finish
If the trip involves any backtracking, curves that don't affect net displacement, or detours, then distance > displacement
solution.finalAnswer: You are calculating the average speed (total distance/time). This equals the magnitude of average velocity only when the trip is taken in a straight line from start to finish, so that the total distance traveled equals the magnitude of the displacement. Any detours, curves, or backtracking will make the average speed greater than the magnitude of average velocity.

hints.hint: Consider what the odometer measures versus what displacement represents.
Think about when the path length equals the straight-line distance.
Imagine driving from city A to city B: when would distance equal displacement?

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 12
title: Instantaneous Velocity vs. Instantaneous Speed
statement: How are instantaneous velocity and instantaneous speed related to one another? How do they differ?

solution.approach: Compare the definitions and properties of instantaneous velocity and instantaneous speed.
steps: Define instantaneous velocity: the velocity of an object at a specific instant in time (vector quantity)
Define instantaneous speed: the magnitude of instantaneous velocity at a specific instant (scalar quantity)
Relationship: instantaneous speed = |instantaneous velocity|
Both represent motion at a specific instant, not over a time interval
Key difference: velocity includes direction, speed does not
Speed is always positive or zero, while velocity can be positive or negative depending on chosen direction
solution.finalAnswer: Instantaneous speed is the magnitude of instantaneous velocity. They are related by: instantaneous speed = |instantaneous velocity|. They differ in that instantaneous velocity is a vector (has magnitude and direction) while instantaneous speed is a scalar (magnitude only). Both describe motion at a specific instant in time, but velocity provides directional information while speed does not.

hints.hint: Think about the relationship between any vector and its magnitude.
Consider whether these quantities can be negative.
Remember that both describe motion at a single instant, not over time.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 13
title: Constant Speed with Non-zero Acceleration
statement: Is it possible for speed to be constant while acceleration is not zero? Give an example of such a situation.

solution.approach: Consider situations where the magnitude of velocity remains constant but the direction changes, requiring acceleration.
steps: Recall that acceleration occurs when velocity changes in magnitude or direction
Consider uniform circular motion as an example
In circular motion, speed (magnitude of velocity) can remain constant
However, the direction of velocity continuously changes
Since velocity is changing direction, acceleration must be present (centripetal acceleration)
The acceleration points toward the center of the circular path
solution.finalAnswer: Yes, it is possible for speed to be constant while acceleration is not zero. Example: An object moving in uniform circular motion, such as a car driving around a circular track at constant speed. Although the speed remains constant, the velocity vector continuously changes direction, requiring centripetal acceleration directed toward the center of the circle. The acceleration changes the direction of motion but not the magnitude of velocity.

hints.hint: Think about motion in a circle at constant speed.
Remember that velocity is a vector - it can change even if speed doesn't.
Consider what type of acceleration is needed to keep an object moving in a circle.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 14
title: Constant Velocity with Non-Zero Acceleration
statement: Is it possible for velocity to be constant while acceleration is not zero? Explain.

solution.approach: Analyze the definitions of velocity and acceleration to determine if they can have these characteristics simultaneously.
steps: Recall that acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity: $a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$
If velocity is constant, then $\Delta v = 0$ for any time interval $\Delta t$
This means $a = \frac{0}{\Delta t} = 0$
Therefore, if velocity is constant, acceleration must be zero
solution.finalAnswer: No, it is not possible for velocity to be constant while acceleration is not zero. If velocity is constant, then by definition the acceleration must be zero, since acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.

hints.hint: Think about the definition of acceleration in terms of velocity change.
If velocity doesn't change, what does that tell you about acceleration?

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 15
title: Zero Velocity with Non-Zero Acceleration
statement: Give an example in which velocity is zero yet acceleration is not.

solution.approach: Identify situations where an object momentarily has zero velocity but is still experiencing acceleration.
steps: Consider an object thrown straight upward
At the highest point of its trajectory, the velocity is zero (instantaneously)
However, gravity is still acting on the object, providing a downward acceleration of $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$
This acceleration causes the object to start falling back down
solution.finalAnswer: A ball thrown straight upward has zero velocity at the highest point of its trajectory, but still experiences a downward acceleration due to gravity ($g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$). Another example is a pendulum at the extreme points of its swing.

hints.hint: Think about objects that change direction during their motion.
Consider what happens at the highest point when you throw a ball upward.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 16
title: Direction of Acceleration for Decelerating Train
statement: If a subway train is moving to the left (has a negative velocity) and then comes to a stop, what is the direction of its acceleration? Is the acceleration positive or negative?

solution.approach: Use the definition of acceleration and analyze the change in velocity to determine the direction.
steps: Let's define rightward as positive direction and leftward as negative
Initial velocity: $v_i < 0$ (moving left)
Final velocity: $v_f = 0$ (at rest)
Change in velocity: $\Delta v = v_f - v_i = 0 - v_i = -v_i$
Since $v_i < 0$, we have $\Delta v = -v_i > 0$ (positive)
Acceleration $a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} > 0$ (positive)
Positive acceleration means the acceleration points to the right
solution.finalAnswer: The acceleration is directed to the right (opposite to the initial motion) and is positive. The acceleration opposes the motion to bring the train to a stop.

hints.hint: Consider how the velocity changes from negative to zero.
Acceleration points in the direction of velocity change, not necessarily in the direction of motion.
If velocity becomes less negative (closer to zero), the acceleration must be positive.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 17
title: Signs of Acceleration for Velocity Reduction
statement: Plus and minus signs are used in one-dimensional motion to indicate direction. What is the sign of an acceleration that reduces the magnitude of a negative velocity? Of a positive velocity?

solution.approach: Analyze how acceleration affects velocity magnitude in both positive and negative velocity cases.
steps: Case 1: Reducing magnitude of negative velocity
If $v < 0$ and $|v|$ decreases, then $v$ becomes less negative (closer to zero)
This means $\Delta v > 0$, so acceleration $a > 0$ (positive)
Case 2: Reducing magnitude of positive velocity
If $v > 0$ and $|v|$ decreases, then $v$ becomes smaller
This means $\Delta v < 0$, so acceleration $a < 0$ (negative)
General rule: Acceleration opposing motion reduces speed
solution.finalAnswer: For a negative velocity: the acceleration is positive (opposite direction to velocity). For a positive velocity: the acceleration is negative (opposite direction to velocity). In both cases, the acceleration opposes the direction of motion to reduce the speed.

hints.hint: Think about what happens to the velocity value when its magnitude decreases.
Acceleration that reduces speed always points opposite to the velocity direction.
For negative velocity, reducing magnitude means becoming less negative (moving toward zero).

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 18
title: Information Needed for Kinematic Problem Solving

hints.hint: Start by listing what you know and what you need to find.
Consider the five kinematic variables: position, initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, and time.
Choose equations that avoid variables you don't know and don't need.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 20
title: Acceleration of Rock in Free Fall
statement: What is the acceleration of a rock thrown straight upward on the way up? At the top of its flight? On the way down?

solution.approach: Apply the principle that gravitational acceleration is constant throughout the motion.
steps: On the way up: gravity acts downward, so $a = -g = -9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$
At the top: gravity still acts downward, so $a = -g = -9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$
On the way down: gravity acts downward, so $a = -g = -9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$
The acceleration due to gravity is constant throughout the entire motion
Only the velocity changes; acceleration remains constant
solution.finalAnswer: The acceleration is $-9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$ (downward) throughout the entire motion: on the way up, at the top, and on the way down. Gravitational acceleration is constant and always points toward Earth's center.

hints.hint: Think about what causes the rock's motion to change.
Gravity acts continuously throughout the motion.
Acceleration doesn't depend on the direction of velocity, only on the forces acting.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 21
title: Velocity and Acceleration Analysis for Vertical Motion
statement: An object that is thrown straight up falls back to Earth. This is one-dimensional motion. (a) When is its velocity zero? (b) Does its velocity change direction? (c) Does the acceleration due to gravity have the same sign on the way up as on the way down?

solution.approach: Analyze the velocity and acceleration characteristics throughout the vertical motion.
steps: (a) Velocity is zero at the highest point of the trajectory
At this point, the object momentarily stops before falling back down
(b) Yes, velocity changes direction
Initially positive (upward), becomes zero at top, then negative (downward)
(c) Yes, acceleration due to gravity has the same sign throughout
Acceleration is always $-g$ (downward) on the way up and on the way down
The force of gravity and thus its acceleration never changes direction
solution.finalAnswer: (a) Velocity is zero at the highest point of the flight. (b) Yes, velocity changes direction from upward (positive) to downward (negative). (c) Yes, acceleration due to gravity has the same sign (negative, pointing downward) throughout the entire motion, both on the way up and on the way down.

hints.hint: Think about what happens at the turning point of the motion.
Consider how velocity and acceleration can be different from each other.
Acceleration depends on forces, while velocity depends on motion direction.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 22
title: Rock Speed Comparison: Up vs Down Path
statement: Suppose you throw a rock nearly straight up at a coconut in a palm tree, and the rock misses on the way up but hits the coconut on the way down. Neglecting air resistance, how does the speed of the rock when it hits the coconut on the way down compare with what it would have been if it had hit the coconut on the way up? Is it more likely to dislodge the coconut on the way up or down? Explain.

unknowns.description: speed when hitting coconut on way up
speed when hitting coconut on way down

solution.approach: Use conservation of energy and kinematic equations to compare speeds at the same height on the way up versus way down.
steps: By conservation of energy, at the same height, the rock has the same kinetic energy whether going up or down
Since KE = ½mv², the speed magnitude is the same at any given height on both paths
However, the velocity directions are opposite (up vs down)
For dislodging: The rock has the same speed in both cases, so the impact force would be similar
But psychologically, a falling object might seem more effective due to the downward motion matching gravity
solution.finalAnswer: The speed magnitudes are equal at the same height on both paths. The likelihood of dislodging the coconut is the same in both cases since the impact speed is identical.

hints.hint: Think about conservation of energy - what happens to kinetic and potential energy?
At the same height, the rock has the same total mechanical energy whether going up or down.
Use v² = v₀² - 2gh for upward motion and v² = 2g(h_max - h) for downward motion from the peak.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 23
title: Effect of Air Resistance on Projectile Motion
statement: If an object is thrown straight up and air resistance is negligible, then its speed when it returns to the starting point is the same as when it was released. If air resistance were not negligible, how would its speed upon return compare with its initial speed? How would the maximum height to which it rises be affected?

solution.approach: Analyze the effects of air resistance on both the upward and downward portions of the trajectory using energy considerations.
steps: Without air resistance: By conservation of energy, v_final = v_initial
With air resistance: Air resistance always opposes motion, doing negative work
On the way up: Air resistance acts downward, reducing kinetic energy more quickly
This results in a lower maximum height than without air resistance
On the way down: Air resistance acts upward, reducing the kinetic energy gained
The object returns with less speed than it started with because energy was dissipated by air resistance throughout the entire trip
Maximum height is reduced because less energy is available to convert to potential energy
solution.finalAnswer: With air resistance, the return speed would be less than the initial speed because energy is dissipated by air resistance. The maximum height would also be reduced because air resistance removes energy during the upward journey.

hints.hint: Consider what air resistance does to the mechanical energy of the system.
Air resistance always opposes motion, so it does negative work in both directions.
Think about energy conservation: initial KE = final KE + energy lost to air resistance + PE at maximum height.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 24
title: Safe Fall Height Comparison: Moon vs Earth
statement: The severity of a fall depends on your speed when you strike the ground. All factors but the acceleration due to gravity being the same, how many times higher could a safe fall on the Moon be than on Earth (gravitational acceleration on the Moon is about 1/6 that of the Earth)?

givenValues.description: acceleration due to gravity on Earth
acceleration due to gravity on Moon (g_E/6)

solution.approach: Use kinematic equations to relate fall height to impact speed, then find the ratio of heights for the same impact speed.
steps: For a fall from rest, the final speed is given by: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$
For the same safe impact speed on both Earth and Moon: $v_E = v_M$
Therefore: $\sqrt{2g_E h_E} = \sqrt{2g_M h_M}$
Squaring both sides: $2g_E h_E = 2g_M h_M$
Solving for the height ratio: $\frac{h_M}{h_E} = \frac{g_E}{g_M}$
Substituting values: $\frac{h_M}{h_E} = \frac{g_E}{g_E/6} = 6$
solution.finalAnswer: A safe fall on the Moon could be 6 times higher than on Earth.

hints.hint: Use the kinematic equation relating final velocity to height for free fall from rest.
Set the impact speeds equal and solve for the ratio of heights.
Remember that v² = 2gh for free fall, so if v is the same, then gh must be the same.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 25
title: Astronaut Jump Height: Moon vs Earth
statement: How many times higher could an astronaut jump on the Moon than on Earth if his takeoff speed is the same in both locations (gravitational acceleration on the Moon is about 1/6 of on Earth)?

givenValues.description: acceleration due to gravity on Earth
acceleration due to gravity on Moon (g_E/6)

solution.approach: Use kinematic equations to find maximum height in terms of initial velocity and gravity, then compare the ratios.
steps: At maximum height, final velocity is zero: $v_f = 0$
Using $v_f^2 = v_0^2 - 2gh$, we get: $0 = v_0^2 - 2gh$
Solving for height: $h = \frac{v_0^2}{2g}$
On Earth: $h_E = \frac{v_0^2}{2g_E}$
On Moon: $h_M = \frac{v_0^2}{2g_M}$
Taking the ratio: $\frac{h_M}{h_E} = \frac{\frac{v_0^2}{2g_M}}{\frac{v_0^2}{2g_E}} = \frac{g_E}{g_M}$
Substituting: $\frac{h_M}{h_E} = \frac{g_E}{g_E/6} = 6$
solution.finalAnswer: An astronaut could jump 6 times higher on the Moon than on Earth with the same takeoff speed.

hints.hint: At the peak of the jump, what is the astronaut's velocity?
Use v² = v₀² - 2gh with final velocity equal to zero.
The maximum height is inversely proportional to gravitational acceleration when initial speed is constant.

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 26

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 27

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 30

title: Earth's Speed and Velocity Around Sun
statement: (a) Calculate Earth's average speed relative to the Sun. (b) What is its average velocity over a period of one year?

solution.approach: Calculate average speed using orbital circumference and period, then determine average velocity for complete orbit.
steps: Calculate orbital circumference: $C = 2\pi r = 2\pi(1.50 \times 10^{11}) = 9.42 \times 10^{11}$ m
Calculate average speed: $v_{avg} = \frac{C}{T} = \frac{9.42 \times 10^{11}}{3.16 \times 10^7} = 2.98 \times 10^4$ m/s

Net displacement over one year = 0, therefore average velocity = 0
solution.finalAnswer: (a) Average speed = 2.98 × 10⁴ m/s = 29.8 km/s, (b) Average velocity = 0 m/s

After one complete orbit, Earth returns to its starting position

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 6

statement: A helicopter blade spins at exactly 100 revolutions per minute. Its tip is 5.00 m from the center of rotation. (a) Calculate the average speed of the blade tip in the helicopter's frame of reference. (b) What is its average velocity over one revolution?

solution.approach: Convert rotation rate to standard units, calculate circumference, then find speed and velocity.
steps: Convert frequency to rev/s: $f = \frac{100 \text{ rev}}{60 \text{ s}} = 1.67$ rev/s
Calculate circumference: $C = 2\pi r = 2\pi(5.00) = 31.4$ m
Calculate average speed: $v_{avg} = f \times C = 1.67 \times 31.4 = 52.4$ m/s
For average velocity over one complete revolution: blade tip returns to same position
Net displacement over one revolution = 0, therefore average velocity = 0
solution.finalAnswer: (a) Average speed = 52.4 m/s, (b) Average velocity = 0 m/s

hints.hint: Convert revolutions per minute to revolutions per second first
The blade tip travels the circumference in each revolution
After one complete revolution, the blade tip returns to its starting position

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 39
title: Burt Munro's Motorcycle World Record
statement: In 1967, New Zealander Burt Munro set the world record for an Indian motorcycle, on the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, with a maximum speed of 183.58 mi/h. solution.approach: Find the acceleration rate, then calculate time to reach maximum speed and distance during acceleration, followed by constant speed phase
steps: Calculate acceleration: a = v_{60}/t_{60} = (60.0 mi/h)/(4.00 s) = 15.0 mi/h/s
Convert to consistent units: 15.0 mi/h/s × (1 h/3600 s) = 4.17 × 10^{-3} mi/s²
Time to reach maximum speed: t_1 = v_{max}/a = (183.58 mi/h)/(15.0 mi/h/s) = 12.24 s
Distance during acceleration: d_1 = \frac{1}{2}at_1^2 = \frac{1}{2}(4.17 × 10^{-3})(12.24)^2 = 0.312 mi
Remaining distance at constant speed: d_2 = 5.00 - 0.312 = 4.688 mi
Convert maximum speed: 183.58 mi/h = 0.05099 mi/s
Time at constant speed: t_2 = d_2/v_{max} = 4.688 mi / 0.05099 mi/s = 91.9 s
Total time: t_{total} = t_1 + t_2 = 12.24 + 91.9 = 104.1 s

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 40
title: Usain Bolt's Olympic Records
statement: (a) A world record was set for the men's 100-m dash in the 2008 Olympic Games in Beijing by Usain Bolt of Jamaica. Bolt "coasted" across the finish line with a time of 9.69 s. If we assume that Bolt accelerated for 3.00 s to reach his maximum speed, and maintained that speed for the rest of the race, calculate his maximum speed and his acceleration. (b) During the same Olympics, Bolt also set the world record in the 200-m dash with a time of 19.30 s. Using the same assumptions as for the 100-m dash, what was his maximum speed for this race?

solution.approach: Use kinematic equations for two-phase motion: acceleration phase and constant velocity phase
steps: Part (a): For 100-m dash
Distance during acceleration: d_1 = \frac{1}{2}at_{acc}^2 = \frac{1}{2}a(3.00)^2 = 4.5a
Maximum speed: v_{max} = at_{acc} = 3.00a
Time at constant speed: t_2 = t_{100} - t_{acc} = 9.69 - 3.00 = 6.69 s
Distance at constant speed: d_2 = v_{max} \cdot t_2 = 3.00a \cdot 6.69 = 20.07a
Total distance: d_1 + d_2 = 4.5a + 20.07a = 24.57a = 100 m
Solve for acceleration: a = 100/24.57 = 4.07 m/s²
Maximum speed: v_{max,100} = 3.00 × 4.07 = 12.2 m/s
Part (b): For 200-m dash, assume same acceleration
Distance during acceleration: d_1 = 4.5 × 4.07 = 18.3 m
Time at constant speed: t_2 = 19.30 - 3.00 = 16.30 s
Remaining distance: d_2 = 200 - 18.3 = 181.7 m
Maximum speed for 200-m: v_{max,200} = 181.7/16.30 = 11.1 m/s
solution.finalAnswer: (a) Maximum speed = 12.2 m/s, acceleration = 4.07 m/s². (b) Maximum speed = 11.1 m/s

hints.hint: The motion has two phases: acceleration for 3.00 s, then constant speed
Use the total distance equation: distance during acceleration + distance at constant speed = total distance
For part (b), assume the same acceleration as in the 100-m dash

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 45
title: Dolphin Jump Analysis
statement: A dolphin in an aquatic show jumps straight up out of the water at a velocity of 13.0 m/s. (a) List the knowns in this problem. (b) How high does his body rise above the water? solution.approach: Use kinematic equations for projectile motion with upward initial velocity
steps: Part (a) - Known values:
Initial velocity v₀ = 13.0 m/s (upward)
Acceleration a = -g = -9.80 m/s² (downward)
Final velocity at maximum height v = 0 m/s
Part (b) - Maximum height:
At maximum height, final velocity v = 0
Use equation: v² = v₀² - 2gh
Substitute: 0² = (13.0)² - 2(9.80)h
Solve for h: 0 = 169 - 19.6h
Therefore: h = 169/19.6 = 8.62 m
Units check: m²/s² ÷ (m/s²) = m ✓
Reasonableness: ~8.6 m is reasonable for a dolphin jump
Part (c) - Time in air:
Time to reach maximum height: v = v₀ - gt
Total time in air: t_{total} = 2t₁ = 2(1.33) = 2.66 s
solution.finalAnswer: (a) Known: v₀ = 13.0 m/s, g = 9.80 m/s², v at max height = 0. (b) Maximum height = 8.62 m. (c) Time in air = 2.66 s

Use v² = v₀² - 2gh for part (b) and v = v₀ - gt for part (c)

sourceReference: College Physics for AP Courses 2e, Chapter 2, Problem 46
title: Swimmer Diving Board Analysis
statement: A swimmer bounces straight up from a diving board and falls feet first into a pool. She starts with a velocity of 4.00 m/s, and her takeoff point is 1.80 m above the pool. (a) How long are her feet in the air? (b) What is her highest point above the board? (c) What is her velocity when her feet hit the water?

solution.approach: Use kinematic equations considering the swimmer starts above the pool and ends at pool level
steps: Part (a) - Time in air:
Taking pool level as y = 0, initial position y₀ = 1.80 m
Use equation: y = y₀ + v₀t - \frac{1}{2}gt²
At pool level: 0 = 1.80 + 4.00t - \frac{1}{2}(9.80)t²
Rearrange: 4.90t² - 4.00t - 1.80 = 0
Using quadratic formula: t = \frac{4.00 ± \sqrt{16.0 + 4(4.90)(1.80)}}{2(4.90)}
Taking positive root: t = 11.16/9.80 = 1.14 s
Part (b) - Maximum height above board:
At maximum height, v = 0: v² = v₀² - 2gh_{max}
Part (c) - Final velocity:
Use v² = v₀² - 2g(y - y₀)
v = -\sqrt{51.28} = -7.16 m/s (negative = downward)
solution.finalAnswer: (a) Time in air = 1.14 s. (b) Maximum height above board = 0.816 m. (c) Final velocity = -7.16 m/s

hints.hint: Set up a coordinate system with the pool surface as y = 0
For part (a), use the displacement equation and solve the quadratic equation
The swimmer goes up first, then falls down past the starting point to the pool
